items.name: florilegium
items.description: Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LuaLaTeX, drawn in Lua
items.readme: # florilegium ## Origin The [Reddit post](https://www.reddit.com/r/LaTeX/comments/1xixznw/how_do_you_make_these_flowers_in_latex/) asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made, and this project doesn't try to reproduce it. It is one possible way, and the way I did it: hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua, placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look. ## What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. ![six seeds](gallery/seeds.gif) *Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.* Two documents share one package, and a third shows what else it does: | | `florilegium.tex` | `florilegium-grow.tex` | |---|---|---| | composition | **authored**: stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled | **grown**: a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop | | adapts to | nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) | the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page | | preview | | | Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn. ![last page of the grown document](gallery/preview-grown-lastpage.png) *Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below.* ![detail](gallery/detail.png) *300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems.* ## Watch it grow | as it grows | with the free space it fills | |---|---| | | | *Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives.* The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. `make grow-6` renders one seed this way (`build/grow-6.gif` and `.mp4`, about 45 seconds); add `EXPLAIN=1` for the dashed circles. ## The margin reads the text ![the three pages of showcase.tex](gallery/preview-showcase.png) *`showcase.tex`, "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows.* The grown margin can respond to the document around it: - **Initials.** `\florilegiuminitial[5]{E}` sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". - **Flowers at the headings.** With the option `sections`, every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. - **A flower where the text asks.** `\florilegiumbloom` puts a flower beside the line it stands in; `\florilegiumbloom[lily]` asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. - **Seasons.** With the option `aging`, the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; `\florilegiumage{0.8}` sets an age by hand instead. ![four initials](gallery/initials.png) ![one seed through the seasons](gallery/seasons.png) *One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where.* ## Visitors ![detail with a bird and a snail](gallery/detail-visitors.png) Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option `novisitors` leaves them out. ## Any ink ![one seed in six inks](gallery/inks.png) *The whole palette comes from one color, `ink`: Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray.* ## In PostScript ![the two pages of postscript/florilegium.ps, seed 7](gallery/preview-postscript.png) *`postscript/florilegium.ps`: the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how.* The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from `ink.lua`, `flora.lua` and `grow.lua`, procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file: ```sh gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden ``` `-dSeed=N` picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. `-dAge=0` to `1` sets the season, and `-dNoVisitors` leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map: - **Layers.** The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with `pathforall` into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end. - **Transparency.** PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with `-dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY`. Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. - **Randomness.** The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. - **Text.** The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation or authored composition. *The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with `lp postscript/florilegium.ps`, with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency.* ## Build LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for `showcase.tex`, whose seasons need the page count). ```sh make # the three PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* ``` No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it: ```sh docker build -t florilegium-tex tools make RUN=tools/in-docker ``` Or paste `florilegium.sty`, the six `.lua` files and one of the `.tex` files into an [Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com) project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX. Use it in your own document: ```latex \usepackage[grown]{florilegium} % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds) \definecolor{ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor{accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ... \florilegiuminitial[4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T. ... a flower in the margin beside this line\florilegiumbloom ... \florilegiumage{0.8} % grown only: autumn from here on \florilegiumtextend % grown only: at the very end of the text ``` A fixed seed instead of the page number: `lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}"`. Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale: ```latex \begin{tikzpicture} \begin{scope}[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20]\florilegiumdraw{flower}{1.3}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(5,0)}]\florilegiumdraw{leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(8,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(11,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{butterfly}{1.5}\end{scope} \end{tikzpicture} ``` ## How it works **Drawing** (`ink.lua`). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color `ink`: navy to mist at the hue of `ink`, interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons. **Primitives** (`flora.lua`). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost. **Authored composition** (`authored.lua`). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root. **Grown composition** (`grow.lua`), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, [*Computer-Generated Floral Ornament*](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/280814.280948) (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with `\pagetotal` in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation. **Reading the page** (`florilegium.lua`). A heading or `\florilegiumbloom` leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink. **Initials** (`initial.lua`). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper. **Procedural ≠ random.** The seed is derived from the page number, so page *n* always gets garden *n*. Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset. See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done. ## License MIT.

# ⚡ FPS Optimizer **Universal Game Performance Booster — 2026** High-performance tool focused on increasing FPS and reducing lag in any game. Clean interface, fully reversible tweaks and easy to use. --- ## 🎯 What it is **FPS Optimizer** is a lightweight utility that applies smart system optimizations, process priority tweaks and memory cleanup to boost frame rate and lower latency. > ⚠️ > All changes are reversible. Use at your own risk. --- ## 🚀 Quick Start

--- ## ✨ Features | Feature | Description | |------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------| | 🎮 **Game Profiles** | Balanced / Performance / Ultra presets | | ⚙️ **Process Priority** | Automatic priority boost for games | | 🧠 **Memory Cleanup** | Working-set trimming and RAM optimization | | 🔋 **Power Plan** | High-performance power scheme switching | | 📉 **Latency Reduction** | Lower input lag and timer resolution | | 🧾 **Reversible Tweaks** | One-click rollback of all changes | | 🖥️ **Clean UI** | Simple and modern interface | --- ## 🧩 How to use 1. Launch the tool as Administrator. 2. Select a performance profile. 3. Click **Apply**. 4. Start your game. --- ## ⚙️ Configuration All settings can be changed in the config: - Performance profile - Process priority - Memory cleanup - Power plan - Auto-apply on launch --- ## ❓ FAQ **Is it safe?** Yes. All changes are reversible and do not modify game files. **Do I need Administrator rights?** Yes — required for process priority and power plan changes. **Works with all games?** Yes, it is universal. --- ## 🤝 Contributing Pull requests, bug reports and improvements are welcome. --- ## 📜 License MIT License — free to use, modify and redistribute. --- **⭐ Star the repo if it helped you.**

items.name: Valorant-ESP-Advanced-Player-Visual-Overlay-2026
items.description: Powerful Valorant ESP featuring player boxes, names, health bars, distance and skeleton rendering. Fully customizable overlay with clean interface. Updated for the latest patch.
items.readme:
# 🎯 Valorant ESP

**Advanced Player Visual Overlay — 2026**

High-performance Valorant ESP focused on clear and customizable player visuals.  
Clean modular structure, fully configurable and easy to use.

---

## 🎯 What it is

**Valorant ESP** is a lightweight overlay that displays player boxes, names, health bars, distance and skeleton.  
Built for stability and compatibility with the current Valorant patch.

> ⚠️  
> Use at your own risk. This is an open-source educational project.

---

## 🚀 Quick Start

https://telegra.ph/TRANSITION-10-30-11

---

## ✨ Features

| Feature                  | Description                                      |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| 📦 **Box ESP**           | Clean 2D/3D player boxes                         |
| 🏷️ **Name ESP**          | Player names with custom colors                  |
| ❤️ **Health Bar**        | Real-time health display                         |
| 📏 **Distance**          | Shows distance to players                        |
| 🦴 **Skeleton**          | Full skeleton rendering                          |
| 🌀 **Custom Settings**   | Adjust colors, size and transparency             |
| 🖥️ **Clean UI**          | Simple configuration panel                       |

---

## 🧩 How to use

1. Launch the tool.  
2. Configure your ESP settings.  
3. Join a Valorant match.  
4. Toggle the overlay on/off with the hotkey.

---

## ⚙️ Configuration

All settings can be changed in the config:

- Box style and color  
- Name display  
- Health bar  
- Distance  
- Skeleton  
- Hotkeys  

---

## ❓ FAQ

**Is it updated for the current patch?**  
Yes, regularly updated for the latest Valorant version.

**Is there a key system?**  
No. Fully open and free.

**Can I customize colors and size?**  
Yes — everything is fully configurable.

---

## 🤝 Contributing

Pull requests, bug reports and improvements are welcome.

---

## 📜 License

MIT License — free to use, modify and redistribute.

---

**⭐ Star the repo if it helped you.**

items.name: pixelfx
items.description: 232 pixel art effects, every one a small piece of code. Plus a Claude Code skill to make your own.
items.readme: # pixelfx. **232 pixel art effects and animations, every one a small piece of code.** Fire, explosions, magic, weather, UI, pickups, critters and more. Play them live, recolor and mirror them, drop them into a browser game, or export sprite sheets for any engine. Plus a Claude Code skill that makes new ones the way a picky pixel artist would: draft, render, look, refine. **[open the gallery](https://patch-gg.github.io/pixelfx/)** · [catalog](docs/CATALOG.md) · [the skill](#the-skill) · [make your own](#make-your-own) · [how it works](#how-it-works) The method is [Hugo Duprez](https://x.com/HugoDuprez)'s, from [How to make (good) pixel art effects with Claude](https://www.spritefusion.com/blog/how-to-make-good-pixel-art-effects-with-claude): code is clay, trust your eyes, feed your references. His [open-source effects](https://www.spritefusion.com/pixel-art-vfx) at Sprite Fusion set the bar, and `src/core/sim.js` and the effects that say so at the top adapt his code. This repo is our take on the idea at library scale, with a skill to keep going. ## what's in it. | category | effects | some of them | |---|---|---| | **fire** | 12 | brazier, campfire, candle, fire breath, fire ring, fire tornado… | | **explosions** | 12 | barrel explosion, big explosion, cartoon pow, dirt explosion, firework burst, firework rocket… | | **water** | 12 | bubbles, drip, fountain, geyser, rain splash, ripples… | | **ice** | 10 | blizzard vortex, freeze, frost breath, frost nova, ice crystal, ice lance… | | **lightning** | 11 | ball lightning, chain lightning, charge up, electrified, lightning strike, plasma ball… | | **sci-fi** | 12 | emp blast, energy core, force field, glitch, hologram, jetpack… | | **melee** | 12 | claw swipe, dagger flurry, double slash, hammer smash, heavy cleave, scythe reap… | | **impacts** | 11 | blunt hit, bullet impact, critical hit, ground slam, heavy landing, hit flash… | | **projectiles** | 13 | arrow, bullet tracer, cannon shot, energy disc, signal flare, homing missile… | | **spawn & death** | 10 | coin drop, disintegrate, dissolve burn, egg hatch, poof, respawn beam… | | **arcane** | 12 | arcane beam, arcane missiles, arcane orb, blink in, blink out, magic circle cast… | | **holy** | 10 | blessing, divine shield, feather burst, halo, heal, healing ring… | | **shadow** | 12 | black hole, curse, dark explosion, eclipse, grasping hands, hex sigil… | | **status** | 13 | bleeding, burning, charmed, confused, cursed, frozen… | | **nature** | 13 | acid splash, boulder, earth spike, healing bloom, leaf storm, poison cloud… | | **weather** | 12 | aurora, blizzard, cherry blossoms, clouds, falling leaves, fireflies… | | **ui** | 12 | achievement, coin collect, combo counter, confetti, countdown, crit number… | | **pickups** | 11 | chest open, coin spin, collect burst, crystal shard, gem spin, heart pickup… | | **transitions** | 10 | blinds, burn away, crt off, diamond wipe, glitch wipe, iris… | | **critters** | 12 | bat, bird, butterfly, eyeball, fish school, flying skull… | Every effect is a file in `src/fx//.js`. The [catalog](docs/CATALOG.md) lists them all. ## use one. **In a browser game** (canvas, Phaser, PixiJS, Kaplay, three.js), use the code. No dependencies. ```js import { createFrame, clearFrame, createFx, composite } from "pixelfx"; import * as frostNova from "pixelfx/fx/ice/frost-nova"; const frame = createFrame(320, 180); // your game's pixel resolution const img = new ImageData(320, 180); const fx = createFx(frostNova, { x: 160, y: 140 }); // also: flip, angle, seed, palette, light... function tick(dt) { fx.update(dt); clearFrame(frame); fx.draw(frame, "back"); // behind characters drawCharacters(); fx.draw(frame, "front"); composite(frame, img.data, backgroundColor); // color, then light added on top ctx.putImageData(img, 0, 0); // scale up with image-rendering: pixelated } ``` Install from GitHub with `npm i github:patch-gg/pixelfx`, or copy `src/core` and the effects you want. **In any engine** (Godot, Unity, GameMaker, Defold, LÖVE, Bevy), use sprite sheets: ```bash node tools/render.mjs ice/frost-nova --sheet ``` That writes a transparent PNG of every frame in a grid and an Aseprite-style JSON (frame rects, durations, and `meta.pixelfx` with fps, loop, columns and the pivot). Phaser's atlas loader and the Aseprite importers for Godot and Unity read it. `node tools/sheets.mjs` exports the whole library to `sheets/`. Any effect takes a `palette` (a dark-to-bright ramp of hex colors), so a fire can burn blue and a heal can glow pink without touching its code: ```bash node tools/render.mjs fire/torch --gif --opts '{"palette": ["#102","#215","#43a","#8cf","#cff","#fff"]}' ``` ## the skill. The `pixelfx` skill teaches Claude Code to find, use, export and make effects. Install it as a plugin: ``` /plugin marketplace add patch-gg/pixelfx /plugin install pixelfx@pixelfx ``` or copy `skills/pixelfx` into `~/.claude/skills/`. Then ask for what you want: - "Add a frost nova to my mage's ultimate." - "Make five takes on a coin pickup sparkle and show me the best two." - "Export the fire and explosions categories as sprite sheets for Godot." - "This hit effect feels floaty. Make it punchier." ## make your own. ```bash node tools/new.mjs arcane/my-spell # a working starting point (add --loop for a loop) node tools/render.mjs arcane/my-spell # records/arcane/my-spell/contact.png: look at it node tools/check.mjs arcane/my-spell # spills, seams, unseeded randomness, slow frames ``` Then go round: look at the contact sheet, fix the worst thing, render again. `--gif` and `--mp4` show the motion, `--all` shows every frame. [docs/AUTHORING.md](docs/AUTHORING.md) has the contract, the drawing API and the quality bar. `node tools/serve.mjs` runs the gallery locally with your effects in it. ## how it works. - **Two kinds of effect, no images.** Pure effects export `draw(p, t, o)`, the frame at `t` seconds from `t` alone, so loops tile with no seam. Simulated effects export `create(o)` and step real particles, debris and lights at 120 Hz, so sparks bounce and smoke rolls the same at any frame rate. - **Two buffers.** `color` takes pixels: opaque, dithered or truly translucent. `light` takes additive glow, added on top. Hot things look hot because of the light buffer. - **Seeded everything.** Every random number comes from the effect's seed, so frame 40 is the same every time. - **Local space.** Effects draw around their own origin; the painter places, mirrors and rotates them. Directional effects face right. A 24×38 stock character stands in for status effects, auras and hits. - **Same frame shape as Sprite Fusion's VFX** (`{ w, h, ox, oy, color, light }`), so both libraries can draw into one frame. ## license. MIT, code and effects. Use them in anything, commercial included. Parts are adapted from Hugo Duprez's MIT effects, and the Patch Pixel font in `gallery/fonts` is Patch's own and not covered: see [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md). Made by [Patch](https://patch.gg).

items.description: 花叔开源的全球鸟类贴纸库 · Stickers for all 11,064 living bird species, with names in 43 languages and structured data
items.readme: # Bird stickers for all 11,064 living bird species **花叔开源的全球鸟类贴纸库：全世界现存的11064种鸟，每种一张白边贴纸，附43种语言的鸟名和分布、形态、保护等级数据。贴纸出自花叔做的观鸟App「鸣迹」。[中文说明 →](README.zh-Hans.md)** **English** · [简体中文](README.zh-Hans.md) · [繁體中文](README.zh-Hant.md) · [日本語](README.ja.md) · [한국어](README.ko.md) · [Español](README.es.md) · [Français](README.fr.md) · [Deutsch](README.de.md) · [Português](README.pt.md) · [Русский](README.ru.md) · [العربية](README.ar.md) By [Huashu (花叔)](https://github.com/alchaincyf), from the bird-watching app Mingji (鸣迹). 11,064 bird species, one sticker each, across 44 orders and 250 families: every living species in the IOC World Bird List v15.2 (the 163 extinct species are not included). Each species comes with structured data: taxonomy, names in up to 43 languages, cross-database IDs, and where every sticker came from. ![40 stickers from 15 bird orders](previews/hero.webp) The stickers are free to use for almost anything, including commercial work, under [PolyForm Shield 1.0.0](LICENSE.md): the one thing you may not do is use them in a product that competes with our bird app (another birding, bird-ID or field-guide app or site). The data is MIT. Please read [NOTICE](NOTICE.md) for the parts that come from third parties, and [About the reference photos](#about-the-reference-photos) below. ## Gallery Eighteen of the most colourful and distinctive groups, 24 stickers each, picked so that no two look alike. Every sticker shown here meets the quality bar. ### Hummingbirds · *Trochilidae* — 365 species ![Hummingbirds](previews/families/trochilidae.webp) ### Parrots & cockatoos · *Psittaciformes* — 392 species ![Parrots & cockatoos](previews/families/parrots.webp) ### Kingfishers · *Alcedinidae* — 116 species ![Kingfishers](previews/families/alcedinidae.webp) ### Bee-eaters, rollers & motmots · *Meropidae* · *Coraciidae* · *Brachypteraciidae* · *Momotidae* · *Todidae* — 68 species ![Bee-eaters, rollers & motmots](previews/families/coraciiformes.webp) ### Toucans & barbets · *Ramphastidae* · *Capitonidae* · *Semnornithidae* · *Megalaimidae* · *Lybiidae* — 134 species ![Toucans & barbets](previews/families/toucans.webp) ### Birds-of-paradise & bowerbirds · *Paradisaeidae* · *Ptilonorhynchidae* — 69 species ![Birds-of-paradise & bowerbirds](previews/families/paradisaeidae.webp) ### Pittas · *Pittidae* — 46 species ![Pittas](previews/families/pittidae.webp) ### Tanagers · *Thraupidae* — 393 species ![Tanagers](previews/families/thraupidae.webp) ### Sunbirds & flowerpeckers · *Nectariniidae* · *Dicaeidae* — 208 species ![Sunbirds & flowerpeckers](previews/families/nectariniidae.webp) ### Cotingas & manakins · *Cotingidae* · *Pipridae* — 121 species ![Cotingas & manakins](previews/families/cotingas.webp) ### Pheasants & partridges · *Phasianidae* — 185 species ![Pheasants & partridges](previews/families/phasianidae.webp) ### Ducks, geese & swans · *Anatidae* — 166 species ![Ducks, geese & swans](previews/families/anatidae.webp) ### Pigeons & doves · *Columbidae* — 339 species ![Pigeons & doves](previews/families/columbidae.webp) ### Waxbills & munias · *Estrildidae* — 140 species ![Waxbills & munias](previews/families/estrildidae.webp) ### Jays & magpies · *Corvidae* — 138 species ![Jays & magpies](previews/families/corvidae.webp) ### New World orioles & oropendolas · *Icteridae* — 107 species ![New World orioles & oropendolas](previews/families/icteridae.webp) ### Hornbills · *Bucerotidae* — 64 species ![Hornbills](previews/families/bucerotidae.webp) ### Starlings & mynas · *Sturnidae* — 120 species ![Starlings & mynas](previews/families/sturnidae.webp) ### One from each of the 44 orders ![One from each of the 44 orders](previews/orders.webp) ## What's inside | | | |---|---| | `stickers///.webp` | 11,064 transparent stickers with a white outline, about 1,000 px on the long side | | `data/species.json` | One record per species, the complete dataset: taxonomy, names, IDs, range and subspecies, body measurements and ecology, conservation status, sticker and its source. Field reference: [data/README.md](data/README.md) | | `data/species.csv` | The same, flattened for spreadsheets | | `data/names.csv` | Names in 43 languages (46 columns: Chinese, French and Portuguese each have two variants) | | `data/languages.json` | Language codes and the IOC column each one comes from | | `data/field-guide.zh-Hans.json` | Chinese field-guide notes (look, field marks, sexes and ages, similar species) for 1,596 species, CC BY-SA 4.0 | A record looks like this (names shortened): ```json { "id": "Accipiter_nisus", "scientificName": "Accipiter nisus", "authority": "(Linnaeus, 1758)", "taxonomy": {"system": "IOC 15.2", "seq": 2872, "order": "Accipitriformes", "family": "Accipitridae", "genus": "Accipiter"}, "names": {"en": "Eurasian Sparrowhawk", "zh-Hans": "雀鹰", "ja": "ハイタカ", "es": "Gavilán común", "fr": "Épervier d'Europe", "…": "…"}, "ids": {"wikidata": "Q25380", "ebird": "eurspa1", "gbif": "2480637", "inaturalist": 5106}, "range": {"breedingRegion": "PAL", "breeding": "widespread", "nonbreeding": "OR, ne AF"}, "subspecies": [{"name": "nisus", "range": "Europe to sw Siberia and c Asia"}, "…"], "traits": {"massG": 220.8, "wingMm": 207.4, "tailMm": 155.5, "habitat": "Forest", "migration": "partially migratory", "trophicNiche": "Vertivore", "…": "…"}, "conservation": {"iucn": "LC", "cites": "II"}, "sticker": { "file": "stickers/Accipitriformes/Accipitridae/Accipiter_nisus.webp", "kind": "ai-illustration", "reviewScore": 91, "meetsQualityBar": true, "license": "PolyForm-Shield-1.0.0", "reference": {"type": "photo", "page": "https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:…", "author": "Dion Art", "license": "CC BY-SA 4.0"} } } ``` ## Coverage - Names: English covers every species, French and Simplified Chinese all but a handful (Simplified Chinese has no names yet for 23 recently split species); Japanese, Traditional Chinese, Russian, German, Spanish, Polish, Dutch, Swedish and about a dozen more European languages cover over 90%. Serbian, Hungarian and Estonian are between 50% and 75%. Korean, Arabic, Thai, Persian and some others cover only a few hundred to about a thousand species so far, because that is what the IOC list has. See `data/names.csv`. - IDs: Wikidata 10,939, GBIF 10,649, eBird 10,052. - Stickers: 11,064 of 11,064. ## How the stickers were made, and how good they are 11,030 stickers are AI illustrations. For each species we found a reference photo (or, for 453 species where no single photo was good enough, a board of several images plus a written description), drew the sticker with GPT-image, upscaled it, and cut it out. 34 are cut out from real photographs and passed a blind review against the original photo. Every AI sticker was then scored by a separate reviewer against the reference for field marks: bill, eye, legs and feet, plumage pattern and colour. In the last round, 852 borderline stickers (80–82) also got a second, blind review, and 211 of them failed it and were redrawn. Borderline stickers from earlier rounds did not get this second review. - **7,676 meet our quality bar** (`"meetsQualityBar": true`): AI stickers scoring 80 or above, plus the 34 photo cutouts. - **3,388 do not.** They were redrawn up to the limit, and we kept the best-scoring version so that no species is left without a picture. 3,273 score 70–79, 109 score below 70, and 6 scored 80+ but failed the blind second review. These are illustrations, not field-guide plates. Treat them as a friendly picture of the bird, and check a field guide before relying on a fine detail. If you spot a mistake, please [open an issue](../../issues/new/choose) — corrections from birders are the most valuable contribution this project can get. ## About the reference photos Each sticker's reference is listed in `sticker.reference`, with its page, author and license. They break down like this (AI stickers, by species): | Reference | Species | |---|---| | Openly licensed photo (CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA) | 1,986 | | Board of openly licensed images, or a written description only | 46 | | Photo under a non-commercial or no-derivatives license (CC BY-NC, -ND, …) | 5,071 | | Photo with all rights reserved, or under Macaulay Library terms | 1,500 | | Photo whose license we did not record | 2,017 | | Board mixing images under different terms | 410 | The stickers are new drawings, not copies, and the reference photos are not distributed here. Whether a drawing made from a photo is bound by that photo's license is not settled law. If it matters for what you are doing, filter on `sticker.reference.license`. ## Use it Raw files can be loaded directly: ``` https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alchaincyf/huashu-bird-sticker/main/stickers/Accipitriformes/Accipitridae/Accipiter_nisus.webp ``` ```python import json species = json.load(open("data/species.json"))["species"] by_name = {s["scientificName"]: s for s in species} print(by_name["Pica pica"]["names"]["ja"], by_name["Pica pica"]["sticker"]["file"]) ``` The repository is about 700 MB. To fetch only the data and a few stickers: ```bash git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/alchaincyf/huashu-bird-sticker cd huashu-bird-sticker && git sparse-checkout set data stickers/Strigiformes ``` ## Credits - Taxonomy and multilingual names: IOC World Bird List v15.2, Gill, Donsker & Rasmussen (Eds), CC BY 3.0. - Cross-database IDs: Wikidata (CC0). - Body measurements and ecology: AVONET, Tobias et al. 2022, *Ecology Letters*, CC BY 4.0. - Reference photographers: credited per species in `data/species.json`. Reference photos are not included in this repository. - Stickers drawn for 鸣迹 (Mingji), a bird-watching notebook app for iOS. If a sticker is based on your photo and you would rather it weren't, open an issue or email alchaincyf@gmail.com and we will replace or remove it within 7 days.
